screens.title: Introduction to Inheritance: Extending Classes
screens.narratorSegment: In this lesson we open the doors to inheritance in Java, a foundational object-oriented tool that helps you share code and express relationships. Inheritance models an "is-a" relationship: a specialized class reuses fields and methods from a more general class. Practically this means you can avoid repeating core behavior and instead focus on what’s unique. You will learn how to declare inheritance with the extends keyword, how the subclass gains access to public and protected members, and why private members remain encapsulated. We will also cover how constructors are chained and how to use super to call the superclass constructor or reference superclass behavior. Real code examples include a LibraryItem base class and a Book subclass that reuses borrow and return logic. Finally, we’ll highlight when inheritance is the right design choice and common mistakes such as confusing "is-a" with "has-a." By the end you’ll be able to identify suitable inheritance relationships, write constructors that call super correctly, and reason about when to prefer composition over inheritance. Ready to explore inheritance and make your code clearer and more reusable?

screens.title: What you'll be able to do
screens.narratorSegment: These objectives map directly to practical skills you'll use when designing Java classes. First, you will be able to explain what inheritance means and why it matters for code reuse and hierarchical design. This goes beyond a definition: you'll describe how fields and methods flow from a superclass into a subclass and why that reduces redundancy. Second, you'll practice using the extends keyword to express an "is-a" relationship. You will write subclasses that inherit behavior and verify the relationship is appropriate. Third, you'll learn to use super correctly to chain constructors and to access immediate superclass members. You will see how missing a super call can create a compile error if the superclass lacks a default constructor. Fourth, you'll identify when inheritance is suitable and when composition is better, avoiding the common mistake of using inheritance for a has-a relationship. Each objective includes a small mnemonic or visual cue to help you remember the rule and a verified competency milestone so you know when you have mastered that skill. By the end, you'll have both conceptual clarity and practical examples to test in code.

screens.title: What is inheritance?
screens.narratorSegment: Inheritance is an object-oriented mechanism where one class acquires the properties and behaviors of another. In Java, a subclass inherits fields and methods from its superclass, enabling code reuse and clearer hierarchical design. Think of it like a family tree: children inherit traits from their parents but can add or override features. That analogy helps you remember which relationships belong to inheritance: the subclass should truly be a specialized type of the superclass. The practical benefit is that shared behavior is written once in the superclass and used across many subclasses, reducing duplication and easing maintenance. For example, a LibraryItem can implement borrowItem and returnItem once; Book and DVD then reuse those methods rather than each re-implementing borrowing logic. A key nuance is member visibility: public and protected members are accessible to subclasses, while private members remain encapsulated and must be exposed through methods if needed. A common misconception is treating inheritance as a general reuse tool for any shared code; instead, it models an is-a relationship. Always ask: does the subclass really represent a specialized version of the superclass? If yes, inheritance often makes sense. If not, prefer composition. To check your understanding, can you name a case in your codebase where an is-a relationship is appropriate?

keyIdea.title: Definition
keyIdea.text: Inheritance models an is-a relationship so subclasses can reuse fields and methods from a superclass.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.1 › What is inheritance?
Definition

Inheritance explained

A subclass gets fields and methods from a superclass, forming an is-a relationship and enabling code reuse and clearer hierarchies.

Why it matters
  • Reduce duplication by implementing behavior once in the superclass.
  • Create logical hierarchies that reflect domain models.
  • Allow polymorphic use of objects that share a common base.
Key Takeaway

Use inheritance for true is-a relationships to share behavior and state safely.

Analogy & Example
Family tree analogy

Child classes inherit common traits from parent classes, but can add or override methods.

Concrete code idea

LibraryItem defines borrowItem and returnItem once. Book reuses these and adds author and pageCount.

Quick check

Ask: does X truly is-a Y? If yes, inheritance helps. If not, prefer composition where an object has another object as a field.

screens.title: Using the extends keyword
screens.narratorSegment: The extends keyword in Java declares that one class derives from another. When you write ClassB extends ClassA, ClassB becomes the subclass and ClassA the superclass. This declaration immediately gives ClassB access to ClassA's public and protected fields and methods. Practically, you write extends in a class header and then treat the subclass as a more specific type. A concrete example is class Book extends LibraryItem; Book then can call borrowItem without redefining it. A common misconception is that extends copies code into the subclass; it does not. Instead, the subclass shares the behavior defined by the superclass and may override methods to change behavior. Another practical point is that fields with private visibility remain encapsulated; subclasses should use getters or protected access in the superclass if direct access is needed. To practice, create a base class with shared behavior and then define a subclass with extra fields. Verify compilation and runtime behavior. Remember to model a real is-a relationship and not force extends where composition or delegation would be clearer. The final check is whether instances of the subclass can be used wherever the superclass is expected; if they can, you've modeled a proper hierarchy.

keyIdea.title: Syntax note
keyIdea.text: Declare subclassing with extends; it grants access to public/protected members and expresses an is-a relationship.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.1 › Using extends
Syntax

Class declaration pattern

class Book extends LibraryItem {
  String author;
  int pageCount;

  public Book(String title, String itemID, String author, int pageCount) {
    super(title, itemID);
    this.author = author;
    this.pageCount = pageCount;
  }

  public void displayBookDetails() {
    System.out.println("Book Title: " + getTitle());
  }
}
The extends clause expresses the is-a relationship and makes inherited members available to the subclass.
Process
1
Declare extends
Write class Sub extends Super in the class header.
2
Use inherited members
Call methods or use protected fields from the subclass without redefining them.
3
Override when needed
Provide a new implementation if the subclass must change behavior.
Common mistake

Don't use extends to copy shared code if the relationship is not an is-a. That leads to rigid designs.

screens.title: Which members are inherited?
screens.narratorSegment: Not every member declared in a superclass is equally available to subclasses. Public members are accessible anywhere, including subclasses in other packages. Protected members are accessible to subclasses and classes in the same package, which makes protected a common choice when you expect inheritance. Private members are not directly accessible by subclasses; they remain encapsulated within the superclass and are intended to be manipulated via public or protected methods or getters. This distinction matters because it determines how much of the superclass's state a subclass can depend on. For example, if LibraryItem. itemID is private, Book cannot reference itemID directly; Book must call a getter or the superclass can expose protected access if direct subclass use is intended. A misconception is assuming private members are inherited and directly usable; they are part of the object but not visible to subclass code. Design implication: prefer private fields with protected or public accessors for controlled subclass access. When deciding visibility, balance encapsulation with the need for subclasses to initialize or extend behavior. Finally, remember that inheritance shares behavior but does not grant blind access; access modifiers control interaction surfaces.

keyIdea.title: Access summary
keyIdea.text: Public and protected members are available to subclasses; private members are encapsulated and accessed via methods.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.1 › Which members are inherited?
Quick Reference
  • Public: accessible to subclasses everywhere.
  • Protected: accessible to subclasses and package members.
  • Private: not directly accessible to subclasses; use accessors.
Concrete example
Field visibility effect

If itemID is private in LibraryItem, Book cannot reference itemID directly. If itemID is protected, Book can read it. The behavior of borrowItem and returnItem can still be inherited regardless of itemID's visibility.

Design guideline

Keep fields private when possible and expose controlled methods for subclasses. Use protected sparingly when subclass access is intended.

Misconception

Private members are not visible to subclasses even though they are part of the same object instance.

Key Takeaway

Visibility controls how subclasses interact with superclass state; choose access modifiers with inheritance in mind.

screens.title: Constructors and super()
screens.narratorSegment: Constructors in Java follow a clear initialization order: when you create a subclass object, the superclass constructor is invoked first to ensure the inherited portion of the object is properly initialized. You can let Java insert an implicit call to the no-argument superclass constructor, or you can explicitly call a specific superclass constructor using super(...) as the first statement in the subclass constructor. If the superclass does not provide a no-argument constructor, you must explicitly call super with the proper arguments; failing to do so produces a compile-time error. For example, Book's constructor uses super(title, itemID) to initialize LibraryItem fields before assigning author and pageCount. A common misconception is that subclass constructor runs first; in reality the superclass initialization happens first to set up shared state. Another nuance is that super must be the first line in the constructor when used. Practice by writing a superclass with a parameterized constructor and then creating a subclass that calls super with matching arguments. Observe compilation and runtime behavior to confirm the order and correctness. Constructors and super() means superclass constructors run first; use super(...) as the first statement in a subclass constructor when you need to pass initialization values.. In practical terms, why the superclass constructor runs first and how to call it. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Constructor rule
keyIdea.text: Superclass constructors run first; use super(...) as the first statement in a subclass constructor when you need to pass initialization values.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.1 › Constructors and super()
Rule

Superclass constructor runs first

Always ensure the superclass is initialized before subclass-specific fields are set; use super(...) to pass required values if the superclass has no default constructor.

public class LibraryItem {
  public LibraryItem(String title, String itemID) { ... }
}

public class Book extends LibraryItem {
  public Book(String title, String itemID, String author, int pageCount) {
    super(title, itemID);
    // subclass fields initialized here
  }
}
Pro tip

If you see a compile error about missing constructor calls, check whether the superclass lacks a no-argument constructor and add an explicit super call.

Step-by-step
1
Create superclass constructor
Define required arguments that initialize shared state.
2
Call super from the subclass
Place super(...) as the first statement in the subclass constructor to pass values up.
3
Initialize subclass fields
After super returns, set subclass-specific state.

keyIdea.title: Illustration
keyIdea.text: A concrete example showing that subclasses reuse methods and call super to initialize inherited state.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.1 › LibraryItem & Book
Superclass: LibraryItem
class LibraryItem {
    String title;
    String itemID;
    boolean isBorrowed;

    public LibraryItem(String title, String itemID) {
        this.title = title;
        this.itemID = itemID;
        this.isBorrowed = false;
    }

    public void borrowItem() {
        if (!isBorrowed) {
            this.isBorrowed = true;
            System.out.println(title + " (ID: " + itemID + ") has been borrowed.");
        } else {
            System.out.println(title + " (ID: " + itemID + ") is already borrowed.");
        }
    }
}
Subclass: Book
class Book extends LibraryItem {
    String author;
    int pageCount;

    public Book(String title, String itemID, String author, int pageCount) {
        super(title, itemID);
        this.author = author;
        this.pageCount = pageCount;
    }

    public void displayBookDetails() {
        System.out.println("Book Title: " + getTitle());
    }
}
Example walk-through
  • super(title, itemID) initializes the LibraryItem portion of the object first.
  • Book reuses borrowItem and returnItem without redefining them.
  • If itemID were private, Book would need a getter to read it safely.

screens.title: Is-a vs Has-a
screens.narratorSegment: A critical design decision is whether to model relationships with inheritance or composition. Inheritance models an is-a relationship: a subclass should be a specialized type of its superclass. Composition models has-a: one class contains or references another as a field. The chapter warns against confusing these two. For example, a Car is a Vehicle fits inheritance; a Car has an Engine should be implemented with composition where Car contains an Engine object. Misusing inheritance for has-a relationships can produce rigid and misleading hierarchies. Composition provides greater flexibility because you can change components without altering the class hierarchy. A practical test: ask whether instances of the candidate subclass can meaningfully substitute for instances of the proposed superclass. If substitution makes sense, inheritance may be appropriate. If not, prefer composition. Another subtle point is reuse: while both composition and inheritance can reuse code, inheritance also implies a tight coupling of types and behavior. When in doubt, favor composition for loose coupling and prefer inheritance when you want a true subtype relationship. How would you refactor a has-a relationship that was accidentally implemented with extends?

keyIdea.title: Design rule
keyIdea.text: Use inheritance for substitution (is-a). Use composition when one object contains or uses another (has-a).

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.1 › Is-a vs Has-a
Inheritance (Is-a)

Example: Book is a LibraryItem.

Use inheritance when a subclass can substitute for its superclass and shares behavior conceptually.

Composition (Has-a)

Example: Car has an Engine.

Prefer composition when one class should own or encapsulate another without implying a subtype relationship.

Checklist to choose
  • Can the subclass be used where the superclass is expected? If yes, consider inheritance.
  • Does the relationship represent ownership rather than specialization? If yes, use composition.

screens.title: Common mistakes and how to avoid them
screens.narratorSegment: Beginners often make predictable mistakes when applying inheritance. One widespread error is confusing is-a with has-a, using extends where composition would be a better fit. That can produce rigid hierarchies that are hard to change. Another frequent mistake involves constructors: if a superclass lacks a no-argument constructor, forgetting to call super with the correct arguments leads to a compile-time error. You will see this when the compiler cannot find a matching superclass constructor. A third pitfall is assuming private members are accessible to subclasses; private fields are not visible and must be accessed through getters or protected methods. screens.title: Common assessment: super() initialization
screens.narratorSegment: A common assessment question checks whether you know how to initialize superclass fields from a subclass constructor. If a superclass defines only a parameterized constructor, the compiler does not know how to call a no-argument constructor, and it expects you to explicitly call super with matching arguments. For example, if Animal has a constructor that takes a name, then Dog's constructor must call super(name) before doing subclass-specific initialization. Choosing this option ensures the Object has its superclass state correctly set. Options that try to assign superclass private fields directly or call a constructor like Animal(name) are incorrect syntax or violate encapsulation. When answering such questions, remember the two rules: super(...) must be the first statement in a constructor, and it calls the immediate superclass constructor you specify. Practically, when you design class hierarchies, provide constructors that make initialization straightforward for subclasses or include a default no-argument constructor if appropriate. This reduces friction for subclasses and helps avoid compilation errors during subclass construction. screens.title: When inheritance is appropriate
screens.narratorSegment: There are practical scenarios where inheritance is naturally appropriate. Use extends when you have multiple concrete types that share meaningful behavior and you want to treat them uniformly. For example, in a library system different item types—books, DVDs—share borrow and return behaviors; making them subclasses of LibraryItem keeps that logic centralized. In UI frameworks, component hierarchies often benefit from inheritance for consistent lifecycle methods; however, the chapter focuses on core domain modeling where inheritance represents specialization. Another positive pattern is when shared operations are semantically the same across types, such as calculating a total cost or formatting a display string. Even then, keep an eye on future flexibility: if the relationship is likely to change or you expect different contained parts, composition may be safer. A quick rule: if you need polymorphic behavior where instances of subclasses are used through superclass references, inheritance is a strong candidate. When you adopt inheritance, keep constructors well-defined and accessors controlled to maintain encapsulation across the hierarchy. fullNarratorScript:
In this lesson we open the doors to inheritance in Java, a foundational object-oriented tool that helps you share code and express relationships. Inheritance models an "is-a" relationship: a specialized class reuses fields and methods from a more general class. Practically this means you can avoid repeating core behavior and instead focus on what’s unique. You will learn how to declare inheritance with the extends keyword, how the subclass gains access to public and protected members, and why private members remain encapsulated. We will also cover how constructors are chained and how to use super to call the superclass constructor or reference superclass behavior. Real code examples include a LibraryItem base class and a Book subclass that reuses borrow and return logic. Finally, we’ll highlight when inheritance is the right design choice and common mistakes such as confusing "is-a" with "has-a." By the end you’ll be able to identify suitable inheritance relationships, write constructors that call super correctly, and reason about when to prefer composition over inheritance. Ready to explore inheritance and make your code clearer and more reusable?

These objectives map directly to practical skills you'll use when designing Java classes. First, you will be able to explain what inheritance means and why it matters for code reuse and hierarchical design. This goes beyond a definition: you'll describe how fields and methods flow from a superclass into a subclass and why that reduces redundancy. Second, you'll practice using the extends keyword to express an "is-a" relationship. You will write subclasses that inherit behavior and verify the relationship is appropriate. Third, you'll learn to use super correctly to chain constructors and to access immediate superclass members. You will see how missing a super call can create a compile error if the superclass lacks a default constructor. Fourth, you'll identify when inheritance is suitable and when composition is better, avoiding the common mistake of using inheritance for a has-a relationship. Each objective includes a small mnemonic or visual cue to help you remember the rule and a verified competency milestone so you know when you have mastered that skill. By the end, you'll have both conceptual clarity and practical examples to test in code.

This second objectives slide turns the learning targets into actions you can check in code. First, after studying examples you should be able to write a simple superclass and at least one subclass that uses extends. For example, create a LibraryItem base class and make Book extend it so methods like borrowItem and returnItem can be reused. Second, verify constructor chaining: write a subclass constructor that calls super with appropriate arguments, then try removing that call to see the compilation error when the superclass lacks a no-argument constructor. Third, exercise member access by attempting to read public, protected, and private fields from the subclass; observe what is permitted and what must be accessed through getters. Fourth, run the Shape hierarchy activity provided in this chapter to practice constructor use and area calculations and confirm results printing as expected. Each practice goal includes a short milestone so you can mark a verified competency: working code that compiles and demonstrates inherited behavior, explicit super calls, and a design rationale explaining why inheritance was chosen.

Inheritance is an object-oriented mechanism where one class acquires the properties and behaviors of another. In Java, a subclass inherits fields and methods from its superclass, enabling code reuse and clearer hierarchical design. Think of it like a family tree: children inherit traits from their parents but can add or override features. That analogy helps you remember which relationships belong to inheritance: the subclass should truly be a specialized type of the superclass. The practical benefit is that shared behavior is written once in the superclass and used across many subclasses, reducing duplication and easing maintenance. For example, a LibraryItem can implement borrowItem and returnItem once; Book and DVD then reuse those methods rather than each re-implementing borrowing logic. A key nuance is member visibility: public and protected members are accessible to subclasses, while private members remain encapsulated and must be exposed through methods if needed. A common misconception is treating inheritance as a general reuse tool for any shared code; instead, it models an is-a relationship. Always ask: does the subclass really represent a specialized version of the superclass? If yes, inheritance often makes sense. If not, prefer composition. To check your understanding, can you name a case in your codebase where an is-a relationship is appropriate?

The extends keyword in Java declares that one class derives from another. When you write ClassB extends ClassA, ClassB becomes the subclass and ClassA the superclass. This declaration immediately gives ClassB access to ClassA's public and protected fields and methods. Practically, you write extends in a class header and then treat the subclass as a more specific type. A concrete example is class Book extends LibraryItem; Book then can call borrowItem without redefining it. A common misconception is that extends copies code into the subclass; it does not. Instead, the subclass shares the behavior defined by the superclass and may override methods to change behavior. Another practical point is that fields with private visibility remain encapsulated; subclasses should use getters or protected access in the superclass if direct access is needed. To practice, create a base class with shared behavior and then define a subclass with extra fields. Verify compilation and runtime behavior. Remember to model a real is-a relationship and not force extends where composition or delegation would be clearer. The final check is whether instances of the subclass can be used wherever the superclass is expected; if they can, you've modeled a proper hierarchy.

Not every member declared in a superclass is equally available to subclasses. Public members are accessible anywhere, including subclasses in other packages. Protected members are accessible to subclasses and classes in the same package, which makes protected a common choice when you expect inheritance. Private members are not directly accessible by subclasses; they remain encapsulated within the superclass and are intended to be manipulated via public or protected methods or getters. This distinction matters because it determines how much of the superclass's state a subclass can depend on. For example, if LibraryItem. itemID is private, Book cannot reference itemID directly; Book must call a getter or the superclass can expose protected access if direct subclass use is intended. A misconception is assuming private members are inherited and directly usable; they are part of the object but not visible to subclass code. Design implication: prefer private fields with protected or public accessors for controlled subclass access. When deciding visibility, balance encapsulation with the need for subclasses to initialize or extend behavior. Finally, remember that inheritance shares behavior but does not grant blind access; access modifiers control interaction surfaces.

Constructors in Java follow a clear initialization order: when you create a subclass object, the superclass constructor is invoked first to ensure the inherited portion of the object is properly initialized. You can let Java insert an implicit call to the no-argument superclass constructor, or you can explicitly call a specific superclass constructor using super(...) as the first statement in the subclass constructor. If the superclass does not provide a no-argument constructor, you must explicitly call super with the proper arguments; failing to do so produces a compile-time error. For example, Book's constructor uses super(title, itemID) to initialize LibraryItem fields before assigning author and pageCount. A common misconception is that subclass constructor runs first; in reality the superclass initialization happens first to set up shared state. Another nuance is that super must be the first line in the constructor when used. Practice by writing a superclass with a parameterized constructor and then creating a subclass that calls super with matching arguments. Observe compilation and runtime behavior to confirm the order and correctness. When in doubt, favor composition for loose coupling and prefer inheritance when you want a true subtype relationship. Let's summarize the three core concepts you should remember. First, inheritance models an is-a relationship where a subclass gains fields and methods from a superclass, enabling reuse and clearer designs. Second, the extends keyword declares that relationship in Java, while the super keyword is used to reference the immediate superclass or to call its constructor; remember super must be the first statement in the subclass constructor when used. Third, visibility matters: public and protected members are accessible to subclasses but private members are not directly accessible and should be exposed through methods if necessary. Keep these concepts in mind when you design class hierarchies, and always test constructor chaining and substitution to ensure correctness.
